episodes.170264: With above normal amounts of atmospheric moisture and an easterly wave still in the area, the active monsoon pattern continued for portions of New Mexico on July 26, 2022. Thunderstorms developed early in the day and became more numerous throughout the afternoon and evening hours. The Calf Canyon burn scar was hit twice with heavy thunderstorms, but only reported rises along Gallinas Creek. Elsewhere, heavy rain caused flash flooding in San Juan County as well as near Glorieta and Tesuque. Note: The Calf Canyon burn scar had previously been referred to as the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar. On July 26, 2022, officials renamed it to the Calf Canyon burn scar, therefore, from here on out, this is how it will be referenced.
episodes.170370: As an area of high pressure remained to the east of New Mexico, an abundant amount of moisture also stayed in place across the desert southwest on July 27, 2022. This led to yet another very active monsoon day across much of northern and central New Mexico. Thunderstorms developed early in the day and wasted no time in impacted the Calf Canyon burn scar. The northern portion of the burn scar was hit hard again, especially near Gascon and Canoncito Creek. Meanwhile, heavy rain also caused flash flooding in Nambe.
episodes.170412: During the afternoon and evening of Tuesday, July 26th, a cold front moved southward across central and southern Minnesota. A line of storms developed and moved southeast across Minnesota and produced a wind gust of 44 mph at the Hutchinson airport. Also, property was damaged at two farms east of Hutchinson, and trees were also damaged farther east.  Both instability and effective wind shear along the front was ample enough to generate organized strong storms, but not enough for severe storms.
episodes.170416: Overnight thunderstorms crossed into southwestern Indiana which caused damaging wind gusts in Knox county around dawn on the 26th, before dissipating as they continued further into central Indiana.
episodes.170434: Isolated thunderstorms moved across parts of southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon of July 27th.
episodes.170437: Precipitable water values in excess of 150% of normal occurred across western Colorado as monsoon moisture continued to stream into the region. As a result, widespread showers and thunderstorms developed. Weak steering flow aloft resulted in slow moving storms. Additionally, storms produced heavy rain. Flash flooding and a debris flow occurred in Ouray County as a result of the heavy rain. Another localized debris flow occurred in Rio Blanco County.
episodes.170523: A vigorous thunderstorm in Cameron County on July 27th produced frequent lightning near the Harlingen and La Feria areas. One such lightning strike struck a power pole just off Interstate 2, very close to KVEO/KGBT, around 2:50PM CDT, which then caused powerlines to fall onto the Interstate. Traffic was diverted around the area as crews worked to replace the line, which was completed around 8:30PM CDT.
episodes.170570: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and early evening of the 27th, along a weak frontal boundary that had pushed into the region. The strongest storms produced damaging wind gusts and hail.
episodes.170744: Isolated minor wind damage accompanied several severe storms. A weak frontal boundary was draped from the Great Lakes region to the Ozarks of Missouri. A small complex of thunderstorms formed along this boundary during the heat of the late afternoon and early evening hours. Surface dew points in the mid to upper 70's contributed to a very unstable atmosphere. Mixed layer capes were over 3000 j/kg.
episodes.170745: A complex of thunderstorms moved east across southern Illinois during the early morning hours. A few of the storms became severe. The complex of storms occurred along a cold front that extended from the Great Lakes to the mid Mississippi Valley. The storms occurred along the southern fringe of a band of stronger 500 mb winds in a region of weak to moderate instability. Due to moist ground from previous thunderstorms, some roads were flooded.
episodes.170990: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind and hail, along with torrential rainfall across the I-25 Corridor and Northeast Plains.  Areas hardest hit included:  eastern Boulder, Douglas, eastern Larimer, Washington and Weld counties.  Hail up to tennis ball size (2.5 inches), was observed near Black Hollow Reservoir east of Fort Collins.  Elsewhere the hail ranged from quarter to golfball size.  The hail damaged homes and vehicles.  Strong winds also produced some tree damage.  Torrential rainfall produced extensive street flooding around Fort Collins.  Torrential rain and small hail also occurred in the town of Estes Park. The hail piled up to a foot deep in spots, and had to be removed using snowplows. People in the community helped drivers dig out cars and clear the roadway on East Elkhorn Avenue.  Minor flooding also occurred in some of the nearby businesses.  Minor flash flooding was also observed in Washington County.
episodes.171189: A frontal boundary remained parked over the Central Appalachians on the last week of July, which kept southwest Virginia suseptible to heavy downpours from daily showers and thunderstorms for a prolonged period of time. Copious amounts of late evening rain on the 27th resulted in nighttime flash flooding in Dickenson County, where pockets of 2 to 4 inches fell. Local creeks and streams rose out of their banks early in the morning of July 28th and resulted in water on roadways and washing out several residential bridges north of Clintwood. High water also entered into the Clintwood Public Library overnight and flooded the first floor of the building.
episodes.171201: A deluge of showers and thunderstorms continuously rocked West Virginia during the final week of July as a stationary frontal boundary remained draped over the state for a prolonged period of time. Waves of energy flowing along the front contributed to these bursts of heavy rainfall, which gradually tarnished soil conditions. Up to 5 inches of rain fell in spots south of the Interstate 64 corridor between July 26th and 27th.||Flash flooding during this time resulted in local creeks and streams rising out of their banks and spilling onto roads, primarily in Mingo, Fayette, McDowell, and Wyoming Counties. The Scarbro community in Fayette County was evacuated during the early morning hours of the 27th due to the abundance of high water impacting the township.
episodes.171347: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail over mainly east-central portions of South Central Nebraska on this late Tuesday afternoon and evening. Scattered thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a frontal boundary between 4PM and 5 PM CDT, mainly along and north of Interstate 80. Some of the thunderstorms became severe around 5:30PM due to the combination of strong instability (2000-3000 J/kg CAPE) and moderate wind shear (30-40 knots). Several instances of golf ball to hen egg size hail (1.75-2.00) occurred with a supercell thunderstorm, most notably across portions of southern Hamilton County. Thunderstorms gradually weakened as they moved southeast, with only quarter size hail reported as activity shifted through Fillmore County. Thunderstorms exited the eastern portions of the local area between 8PM and 9PM.
episodes.171617: Isolated strong to locally severe storms briefly resulted in hail up to the size of quarters and wind gusts near 60 MPH for some communities.
episodes.171618: A few strong to severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Wyoming during the late afternoon and early evening on July 27th. This activity mainly produced strong wind gusts to 60+ MPH, along with a few reports of quarter to golf ball sized hail.
episodes.171695: A stationary front was observed situated south of the Ohio River across northern Kentucky and West Virginia during July 26th when an upper level disturbance approached the state from the west late that evening. A 30 to 35 mph nocturnal low level jet developed just south of the boundary, tapping deep moisture in place across central Kentucky, carrying it northeast toward Greenbrier County, resulting in deep moisture convergence across the area. Precipitable water values were estimated to have risen from around 1.7 inches around 10 pm on the 26th to nearly 2 inches by around 6 am on the 27th, or two standard deviations above normal for late July. Given the latent heat of the tropical air being carried toward southeast West Virginia, most-unstable layer CAPE values were estimated to be between 500 and 1,000 J/Kg just after midnight on the 27th. Soils were already moistened from 0.5 to locally 1.5 inches of rain that fell during early afternoon on the 26th when another round of storms developed across the western part of the county beginning around 10 pm. Perhaps enhanced by upsloping as the storms entered the higher terrain across the western half of the county, the low-topped convection proved to be efficient, producing prolonged 1 to 2 inch per hour rainfall rates in multiple waves. The heaviest rainfall began to diminish by 5 am on the 27th, leaving only residual shower activity after dropping a large swath of 2 to over 4 inches within the 7 hour period.
episodes.171910: An upper level ridge was centered east of the area and another to the west. That put the local area in a region of weakness between them which is an area conducive for higher rain chances. The upper air soundings around that time showed sufficient instability and moisture in place to support numerous thunderstorm development. One storm developed around New Orleans, but didn���t move much despite the general flow of storms to be northwest at around 10 mph. Getting hung up on a sea-breeze boundary was the likely culprit of the storm not moving and producing flash flooding.
episodes.172109: A thunderstorm across Hamilton county produced hail that was near severe criteria.
episodes.172220: A few strong to severe storms developed over southwest and central Missouri on the afternoon of the 27th south of Interstate 44.
episodes.172296: Showers and thunderstorms, some strong, occurred over the higher terrain and adjacent plains during the evening time frame. Most storms were focused along the I-25 corridor, where heavy rain caused flash flooding in several locations in El Paso and Pueblo Counties.
episodes.172309: Central North Carolina was under a mid-level ridge of high pressure over the southeastern US, while the stronger mid-level flow was over the Mississippi Valley into the Mid-Atlantic states. While there was no defined surface boundary, isolated/scattered storms developed in the mid to late afternoon across the area. Another round of more widespread showers and storms tracked from south-central Virginia into the central North Carolina Piedmont and Coastal Plain in the mid to late-evening hours. Several of the storms produced downed trees and resultant power outages.
episodes.172369: During the mid-to-late afternoon hours on July 27th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed immediately ahead of a quasi-stationary surface frontal boundary located near the Ohio River. Across central Kentucky, temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dewpoints in the mid 70s provided copious amounts of instability, with convection having mixed-layer CAPE in excess of 3000 J/kg to work with. During the mid-afternoon period, showers and thunderstorms developed along the Western Kentucky and Bluegrass Parkways and moved steadily to the south and east. The strongest storms produced isolated wind damage, mainly across south central Kentucky. While most of the severe threat subsided during the overnight hours, persistent convection across south central Kentucky created isolated flash flooding issues.||During the evening hours of July 28th, a secondary weak frontal boundary helped to spark convection across portions of Kentucky, causing isolated wind damage in Meade County.
episodes.172403: Scattered thunderstorms with gusty winds moved over the Currituck Sound on July 27.
episodes.172414: During the late afternoon to evening hours of July 26, 2022, strong to severe storms developed over Northern New Mexico and Southeast Colorado moving east to northeast into Western Kansas. As the storms moved over Southern Wichita County, they produced pea to nickel sized hail south-southwest of Leoti, Kansas.
episodes.172501: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with scattered afternoon thunderstorms across the tri-state region. One storm produced some wind damage near Perry.
episodes.172563: Between July 25th and July 30th, 2022, several complexes of training thunderstorms developed south of I-64 and brought heavy rain, deadly flash flooding, and devastating river flooding to eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia. These thunderstorms, at times, caused rainfall rates in excess of 4/hr across complex terrain that led to widespread devastating impacts. While it did not rain continuously during this 4-day stretch, the overwhelming amounts of rain and resultant flooding led to 39 deaths and widespread catastrophic damage. Entire homes and parts of some communities were swept away by flood waters, leading to costly damage to infrastructure in the region. Over 600 helicopter rescues and countless swift water rescues by boat were needed to evacuate people who were trapped by the quickly-rising flood waters. In total, 24 Flash Flood Warnings were issued between July 26th and July 30th. Between the evening of July 27th and the mid-morning hours on July 28th (the peak of the event), 13 warnings were issued, 3 of which were upgraded to a Flash Flood Emergency.||Radar-based rainfall estimates suggest that upwards of 14-16 of rain fell during this 5-day period in a narrow swath, with many more locations receiving 6-10 of rain. Most of this rain fell during the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th, which is when the most devastating impacts were felt. The highest totals occurred across an axis that stretches from northern Clay and southern Owsley counties, east through southern Breathitt and northern Leslie counties, into Perry, Knott and Letcher counties. The highest rainfall total report was from southern Knott County, where 14.00 fell between July 25th and July 29th. This site, a cooperative (COOP) observer at Carr Creek Lake, reported 6.71 from 7am July 28th to 7am July 29th, following a report of 6.50 at that site on the previous day. Another COOP site in Buckhorn reported 8.00 of rain for the 24-hour period ending 7am on July 28th. The rainfall total in Buckhorn from July 25th to July 29th was 11.76. These rainfall values occurring in such a short period of time are incredibly rare: there is less than a 1 in 1000 chance for this much rainfall over five days in a given year.||The incredible rainfall also led to significant rises and flooding on many rivers in eastern Kentucky including on the main stem of the Kentucky River; North, Middle and South forks of the Kentucky River; Red River and Licking River. At Whitesburg, the North Fork of the Kentucky River swelled well above major flood stage, reaching close to 21' before gauge failure (the previous flood of record was 14.7' in 1957). The North Fork of the Kentucky River at Jackson also reached major flood, setting a new record crest of 43.47' (the previous record was 43.1' set in 1939). The river flooding caused a second round of destruction for communities in the region, and caused flooding in downstream areas that did not receive as much rainfall.||*Note* Given the widespread nature and severity of this event - any dollar amount estimated by storm data will not do the event as a whole justice. Since eastern KY was a national declaration, FEMA will be doing a full cost assessment. Will use this data once available for total monetary amounts of damage.||Visit www.weather.gov/jkl/July2022Flooding for more information on the event, as well as pictures and videos of the flooding and damage.
episodes.172654: Another round of heavy rain showers impacted portions of eastern Kentucky during the early morning hours of July 27th, thanks to a lingering and weakening stationary boundary across the region and a strong flow of moisture advection on the heals of SW flow. Several of these heavy rain producers went across portions of Pike County, leading to two reports of flash flooding.
episodes.172775: Deep monsoon moisture moved back into southern New Mexico from the southeast.  Light winds aloft kept storms moving slowly which allowed for heavy rain and flash flooding to occur in Grant and Otero counties.
episodes.172831: Deep monsoon moisture brought thunderstorms and flash flooding to parts of northern Arizona.
episodes.172832: Multiple mesoscale convective vortices (MCVs) were seen across Arizona during the morning. Clearing skies allowed for daytime heating to add to the already unstable atmosphere.  As a result, there were multiple flash floods across the area.
episodes.172910: A big push of monsoon moisture immediately followed the excessive heat event, and stormy conditions persisted into August. Many storms produced flash flooding, and some produced severe weather.
episodes.172964: Tropical moisture coming in from the Bahamas along with a mid to upper level low over the region led to several periods of strong showers and thunderstorms over the coastal and near shore waters of SE Florida.
episodes.172974: Scattered gale-force wind gusts occurred with numerous showers and thunderstorms moving westward with a passing inverted trough.
episodes.173048: An isolated thunderstorm became severe and produced strong winds and a small area of significant damage.

events.narrative: Heavy rain in the Flora Vista to Bloomfield area in San Juan County caused significant flash flooding in the area. A spotter reported that approximately two feet of water covered County Road 3150, rendering it impassable. Two vehicles were washed away and one home was flooded. Near Crouch Mesa, the San Juan emergency manager reported flash flooding over area roadways, and an RV was washed out. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rainfall of 1.83 inches.
Cars stuck in the road at South Academy and Astrozone.
Heavy rainfall of 1.05 inches.
Storm total rainfall of 1.85 inches. 0.5 inches falling within the past hour.
Reports of stranded and submerged cars with streets closed due to high water on the northwest side of Pueblo near Platteville Blvd.
The local fire department reported a funnel cloud northwest of Silver Lake. This was also confirmed by a trained spotter.
Heavy rainfall of 1.50 inches.

There was a 1.5 mile wide north to south swath of wind damage that extended from Nobles Avenue and 177th Street to the 16500 block of O'Day Avenue. The damage area spread eastward for about one mile. A grain bin was blown over, landing on a propane tank. Much of the roof of a large machine shed was blown off and a large door was collapsed inward. Dozens of trees were broken or large branches were downed, and some corn was flattened.
Heavy rainfall of 1.92 inches.
A few trees and at least one power line were blown down in the Perry area.

Several spotters and fire department members reported a funnel cloud southwest of Winsted, near Highway 7 and County Road 15 (Falcon Ave). The funnel was photographed by at least two people, and caught on video (with time stamp) by one spotter. There was a second hand report of it briefly touching down, with two power poles leaning, but upon further investigation, none of the spotters or fire department members could confirm ground contact, nor was the power pole damage able to be confirmed. Satellite imagery was checked but that did not show any apparent tracks. Therefore this was listed as a funnel cloud.
Road flooded near Don Juan Street and Platte Avenue.

Heavy rain of 2 to 3 inches near Lamy and Glorieta caused flash flooding in the area. A CoCoRaHS observer reported that this heavy rain flooded the arroyo in their backyard, forming a lake. Video shared by local broadcast media also showed flash flooding through a property at La Posta Way. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rainfall of 1.80 inches.
Pea to penny sized hail reported. Most of the hail was pea to dime in size.
Water is covering the road on Purcell Blvd. at Interstate 25.
Stockton Hill Rd was closed.
Two barn structures were destroyed.
Flash flooding of roads.
Significant flooding. A creek normally three feet wide and four inches deep is running forty plus feet wide and at least three feet deep.

Heavy rain in the Tesuque and Chupadero areas resulted in flash flooding. North-northwest of Tesuque, an arroyo overflowed its banks and flooded a backyard near the intersection of Tesuque Village Road and Highway 592. Flash flooding and mud flow also trapped 15 cars in a Tesuque market. Near Chupadero, the emergency manager reported that water over Rio En Medio Road in six locations along roadway. Damages are estimated.
Oatman-Topock Hwy was closed just north of I-40.
Flooding along County Road R and the San Luis Peoples ditch near San Luis.

A few people were evacuated from a home that flooded in eastern Chinle near Canyon de Chelly. The time was estimated from radar.
The stream gauge on Cibcue (CBQ) Creek near the confluence with the  Salt River showed a 3.5 foot rise to 2,500 cubic feet per second.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 40 mph/35 knots was measured at the WxFlow site XDGE Biscayne Bay Harbor Pilots.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 42 mph/36 knots was measured at the WxFlow site XBBH in Dodge Island.

events.narrative: A thunderstorm wind gust of 42 mph/36 knots was measured at the WeatherSTEM site 1847W at Delray Beach North. Height of the anemometer is 59 feet.

High water and impassable roads resulted in an evacuation of the Scarbro community. Other roads in the county became flooded and impassable during the early morning hours of the 27th, including Virginia Street, Main Street of Oak Hill, Allman Street, Scarbro Road, White Oak Fork Road, Wolf Creek Road, Shelton Road, and Summerlee Road.
Heavy rain caused a debris flow along Highway 60 near the Greenbrier Hills Golf Club.  The highway was reopened after the debris was cleared.
Runoff from heavy rain overwhelmed the storm drains around Alfredo's Pizza restaurant in Rainelle and caused 10-12 inches of flood water to enter the building.

Big Clear Creek was observed out of its banks in several locations, including flowing rapidly across Route 60 in the community of Rupert.  The road was reopened after flood waters receded, with no damage reported.
Greenbrier County Emergency Management reported that a road near the James River and Kanawha Turnpike was destroyed when Little Sewell Creek overflowed its banks.

The Meadow River in the township of Nallen rose above its 15 foot bankfull level on the morning of July 27th. The river crested at 17.37 feet before returning to its banks later that afternoon. While above its banks, the river spilled onto Chestnut Grove Road and flooded the nearby lumber yard.
Pike County Dispatch reported that Ashcamp Road was closed at the 10000 block due to high water.
Chestnut Grove and a nearby lumber yard flooded from backwater of Meadow River.

Several miles southeast of Marion, trees and large limbs were down. There was shingle damage to a house. Several trees were snapped. A greenhouse was flipped and rolled. The hvac unit of a house was moved off its concrete pad a few feet.
Pike County dispatch reported that Indian Creek Road past Sunny Fork was closed due to high water.
A bridge washed out on Russellville Road.
Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.
Several trees were down between Norris City and Omaha.
Trees were down in the city of Carmi.
Some water was over several roads in the Mt. Carmel area.
Several roads in the Broughton area were flooded. Water was at least a foot deep over Illinois Route 142.

Route 41 near the intersection of Stonehouse Road was closed due to high water. A water rescue of a stranded motorist took place during that morning. Near the town of Oak Hill, high water restricted access to Minden Road where it intersects McKinney Road.
Several inches of water covered numerous roads within the county, including portions of Highways 1, 14, and 45.
The cooperative observe located 1 mile NNE of Mount Olive measured 4.24 inches of rainfall in a 24 hour period.
Little Garden Creek rose out of its banks and flooded Little Garden Creek Road.
Sewell Creek above Little Sewell Creek at Rainelle (RANW2) crested right at flood stage of 14.00 feet at 9:50 am to 10:00 am EDT on the 27th.
High water was observed along several spots within the towns of Delbarton and Red Jacket.

Flash flooding was observed on the northern portion of the Calf Canyon burn scar as heavy rain estimated at 0.75 inches to 1.5 inches fell. The Rito de Gascon rose about four feet and overtopped its banks. Nearby, raging flood waters were observed along a road near Monte Aplanado. The problematic Canoncito Creek also overtopped its banks again which flooded roads and pastures and destroyed fences. Damages are estimated.

events.narrative: A wind gust to 42 knots was measured at the Montrose Harbor Light.
The Gannet Cove mesonet recorded a gust of 40 knots.

A very electric storm over the Harlingen and La Feria area of Cameron County on July 27th produced a lightning strike that struck powerlines just outside of the KVEO news studio. Those powerlines then fell onto Interstate 2, which initially caused a backup on the interstate. Crews worked to clear the lines quickly, but had to close the interstate again that evening to repair the lines. Timing was based on radar, National Lightning Detection Network (NDLN), and a broadcast media report. No injuries, or car accidents were reported as a result of the downed powerlines.

An area of significant wind damage stretched from the Martin County Airport eastward to the intersection of Hopkins Rd and Highway 125. The damage included trees down, some on cars and homes, damage to lightweight structures and sheds, and damage to a solar farm. The estimated wind gusts were between 75 and 80 mph.
Broadcast media shared a video of street flooding at the intersection of Joseph Street and Tchoupitoulas.
A few trees were reported down near the intersection of Coleman Road and Cole Farm Road.

The Meadow River crested at a stage of 13.96 feet at 11:30 pm EDT on the 27th, and remained above 13 feet from 4:20 pm EDT on the 27th to 9:45 am EDT on the 28th.  The river appeared out of its banks at multiple locations along Highway 60 between the communities of Rupert and Rainelle, causing the highway to be closed until flood waters receded.
Flash flooding was reported over Highway 98 five miles east of K'ai'bii'to.  Some roads washed out in the area.
In the town of Hanover, high water obstructed Pad Fork Road for a brief period of time.
A mudslide occurred along County Road 5 near mile marker 12 near Piceance Creek as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
Dispatched reported Highway 35 was washed out from flooding out of Shingle Canyon.

Heavy rain over the Pipeline Fire scar (2022) resulted in 1-2 feet of water flowing in Schultz Creek, over Mount Elden Road, and overwhelming the culvert at Highway 180, and flowing onto the bike path next to Highway 180.  The water flowing over the highway caused a temporary closure.
Several trees were reported down along Highway M.
Pierce Ferry Rd was closed due to flooding of the Archibald Wash.
A microburst wind gust damaged 2 farm outbuildings and downed around a dozen trees at the farm of a NWS COOP observer. Quarter sized hail was also reported during the event.
Several large trees were reported down.
Strong thunderstorm wind blew the roof from a barn, and rolled a camper trailer.
Several large tress were reported down, some on power lines.
A tree was reported down on a house near the intersection of Wildflower Lane and Caval Chub Lake Road.
Flooding of Short Creek closed several streets in Colorado City.
High winds damaged two poultry houses.
Quarter sized hail was reported.
White Hills Rd was closed.
Strong thunderstorm wind snapped several wooden, high power transmission poles.
Flash flooding closed numerous roads in Golden Valley and also left water and debris on Hwy 93.
Several trees were reported down across County Road CC-30.
Heavy rain near Navajo washed out Service Road 9452 as water flowed out of the arroyo due to debris caught in the drainage. Damages are estimated. Time is estimated based on radar.
Video shared by local broadcast media on Twitter showed flash flooding and mud flow along County Road 117S in Nambe. There are no known damages.
A report of at least a foot of running water and debris over the road near the intersection of North Florida Ave and North Scenic Drive on the north side of Alamogordo.
Heavy rain fell just east of Snowflake with 1.22 inches reported.
Several large trees were reported down.
Wind gusts up to 58 MPH and pea sized hail were observed 13 miles north of Alliance.
Trees were reported down on powerlines near the intersection of Martin Creek Road and Bear Pond Road.
A highway sensor from WYDOT recorded a wind gust to 59 MPH approximately 7 miles southeast of South Greeley, south of Cheyenne.
Trees were reported down on powerlines near the intersection of Pocomoke Road and Fred Wilder Road.
Video shared by local broadcast media shows raging water in a rural part of Pojoaque. Time is estimated based on radar data. No damage reported.
Trees were reported down on powerlines near the intersection of US Highway 1 North and Cleghorns 2 Drive in Youngsville.
Cottonwood Rd was closed from Hwy 93 to mile marker 16.
Strong thunderstorm wind blew down power lines, and blew the roof from an outbuilding.
Strong thunderstorm wind damaged the roof of a home, blew a small metal shed across the road, and snapped large tree limbs.
Trees and powerlines were reported down, resulting in power outages on T K Allen Road northeast of Louisburg Ball Airport.
Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a tree onto Old Highway 33.
Power outages were caused by fallen trees on powerlines. This was near the intersection of Leonard Road and Old Benton Way.
Strong thunderstorm wind damaged and destroyed boat docks, and blew down trees.
A trained spotter located 12 miles SSE of Horse Creek measured a wind gust to 75 MPH. No hail.
Trees were reported down on power lines.
Two trees were down near County Road 327 and Highway H.
Quarter sized hail and very strong wind gusts 70 to 75 MPH were reported by Law Enforcement on Warren Air Force Base from 5:40 PM until 5:50 PM MDT.
A tree fell in Windfield.
A tree fell on Home Chapel Road.
Several trees fell at Davis Crossroads in southern Butler County. An older barn was also lost.
Trees were reported down near the intersection of Randolph Pines Road and Ringwood Road in Enfield.
A tree fell and blocked East Brown Street.
Pea sized hail and estimated wind gusts to 60 MPH were reported 2 miles SSW of Cheyenne.
